mcq.q: Which of the following is a key performance drawback of an array-based stack compared to a linked list-based stack?

options.A: Accessing elements in an array takes O(N) time
options.B: Popping an element from an array-based stack is O(N)
options.C: Inserting elements at the top requires shifting elements
options.D: Resizing the stack requires copying all elements to a new array

mcq.answer_text: Resizing the stack requires copying all elements to a new array

options.C: Pointer to the top node is changed, and memory is freed

mcq.answer_text: Pointer to the top node is changed, and memory is freed

sq.q: What are the advantages, disadvantages, and real-world applications of implementing a stack using an array?
answer: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle. When implemented using an array, elements are stored in a contiguous block of memory.
Fast Access: Since an array is index-based, accessing stack elements is quick.
Easy Implementation: Arrays are simple to use and require less programming overhead.
Memory Efficiency (for small stacks): If the maximum size is known, arrays minimize memory fragmentation.
Fixed Size: The stack size is determined at compile-time, leading to Stack Overflow if exceeded.
Memory Wastage: If the stack is underutilized, allocated memory goes unused.
Resizing Issues: If resizing is required, a new larger array must be allocated, and elements must be copied, which is inefficient.
Function Call Management: Stack is used to manage function calls and recursion in programming.
Expression Evaluation: Used in postfix, prefix, and infix expression calculations.
Undo/Redo Operations: Text editors and graphic software use stacks to store previous states.
Backtracking Algorithms: Used in solving mazes, Depth-First Search (DFS), and puzzle solving.
Memory Management: Stack memory is used in system processes to store local variables and return addresses.

sq.q: How does stack implementation using a linked list differ from an array-based stack, and what are its key benefits?
answer: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle . It can be implemented using either arrays or linked lists , each having its own advantages and limitations.
Key Differences Between Linked List-Based Stack and Array-Based Stack
Uses static memory allocation , requiring a fixed size at declaration.
Uses dynamic memory allocation , growing or shrinking as needed.
The size is predefined and cannot be changed at runtime, leading to Stack Overflow if exceeded.
No fixed size; the stack grows dynamically until memory is exhausted.
Can result in memory wastage if the allocated array size is larger than the actual data required.
Uses only required memory , preventing wastage.
Faster since elements are stored contiguously in memory and accessed using an index.
Slower because elements are stored non-contiguously , requiring pointer traversal.
Push (O(1)) if no resizing is needed, but resizing causes O(n) complexity . Pop (O(1)) .
Push (O(1)) and Pop (O(1)) without resizing, as elements are linked dynamically.
Simple to implement since it only requires an array and an index (top).
More complex , as it requires node creation and pointer manipulation.
Requires manual resizing , which involves creating a larger array and copying elements ( O(n) complexity ).
Grows dynamically without any need for resizing.
No extra memory is required apart from the array itself.
Requires additional memory for pointers , increasing overhead.
Stack Overflow occurs when the predefined size is exceeded.
No Stack Overflow , as long as there is available memory.
Can cause Stack Overflow in recursive calls if the array limit is reached.
Efficient for recursion , as memory is allocated dynamically.

lq.q: A hospital maintains a patient record system where patient details are stored using a stack to manage the most recent patient first. The hospital's software developer has implemented this stack using a linked list to handle dynamic memory allocation efficiently. Each time a new patient arrives, their details are pushed onto the stack. When a patient is discharged, their details are popped from the stack. Using a linked list-based stack, implement the following operations: Add a new patient (push operation). Remove the most recently admitted patient (pop operation). Display the current list of patients in the stack. Write a C program to implement this hospital management system using a linked list-based stack and explain how this approach is better than an array-based stack for this scenario.
answer: C program to implement this hospital management system using a linked list-based stack
struct Patient *push(struct Patient *, char[], int, char[]);
// Function to add a new patient to the stack

printf("\n Patient Added: %s, Age: %d, Disease: %s", name, age, disease);
// Function to remove a patient from the stack
printf("\n NO PATIENTS TO DISCHARGE (STACK UNDERFLOW)");
printf("\n Discharging Patient: %s, Age: %d, Disease: %s", ptr->name, ptr->age, ptr->disease);
// Function to display the last admitted patient (top of the stack)
printf("\n Last Admitted Patient: %s, Age: %d, Disease: %s", top->name, top->age, top->disease);
printf("\n %s, Age: %d, Disease: %s", ptr->name, ptr->age, ptr->disease);
how this approach is better than an array-based stack for this scenario:
A linked list-based stack is the best choice for a hospital patient record system because:
✔ Memory is freed when a patient is discharged
✔ Can handle an unpredictable number of patients
Using an array-based stack would restrict the number of patients and lead to memory inefficiencies. Hence, a linked list-based stack provides better flexibility and efficiency for this scenario.
